title: Selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO over co-electrodeposited dendritic core-shell indium-doped Cu@Cu2O catalyst
abstract: Element doping is an effective strategy to enhance the selectivity of electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction. In this work, a dendritic core-shell In-doped Cu@Cu2O catalyst is prepared by co-electrodeposition method on carbon fiber paper for selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO. Faradaic efficiency of producing CO over this dendritic In-doped Cu@Cu2O reaches 87.6 ± 2.2% with total current density of 11.1 ± 0.85mA cm at −0.8 V vs RHE, which outperforms most of the reported Cu-based electrocatalysts. The excellent performance is mainly derived from charge re-distribution and the enhanced intrinsic activity due to the formation of In-doped Cu2O layer. Meanwhile, the Cu/Cu can be adjusted by tailoring the doped-In content. The relatively high ECSA and small charge transfer resistance are also conducive to improve the selectivity and activity. The oxyphilic In metal incorporated into the copper lattice can well stabilize the intermediate *COOH through enhancing interaction with O-ends of *COOH. This work provides a facile approach and a deep insight on design and synthesis of high efficiency hybrid electrocatalysts.

Selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO over co-electrodeposited dendritic core-shell indium-doped Cu@Cu2O catalyst
Miao Wanga, Xiaona Rena, Gang Yuana, Xiaopo Niua, Qingli Xua, Wenluan Gaoa, Shuaikang Zhua, Qingfa Wanga,b,* a Key Laboratory for Green Chemical Technology of the Ministry of Education, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China b Collaborative Innovation Center of Chemical Science and Engineering (Tianjin), Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Co-electrodeposited In-doped Cu@Cu2O Core-shell Dendritic structure CO2 electroreduction
A B S T R A C T
Element doping is an effective strategy to enhance the selectivity of electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction. In this work, a dendritic core-shell In-doped Cu@Cu2O catalyst is prepared by co-electrodeposition method on carbon fiber paper for selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO. Faradaic efficiency of producing CO over this dendritic In-doped Cu@Cu2O reaches 87.6 ± 2.2% with total current density of 11.1 ± 0.85mA cm−2 at −0.8 V vs RHE, which outperforms most of the reported Cu-based electrocatalysts. The excellent performance is mainly derived from charge re-distribution and the enhanced intrinsic activity due to the formation of In-doped Cu2O layer. Meanwhile, the Cu+/Cu0 can be adjusted by tailoring the doped-In content. The relatively high ECSA and small charge transfer resistance are also conducive to improve the selectivity and activity. The oxyphilic In metal incorporated into the copper lattice can well stabilize the intermediate *COOH through enhancing interaction with O-ends of *COOH. This work provides a facile approach and a deep insight on design and synthesis of high efficiency hybrid electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The rapid increase of manmade CO2 emission upsets the natural balance, resulting in serious environmental challenges like global warming. The conversion and storage of CO2 has attracted more attentions. Many approaches have been developed to convert carbon dioxide as carbonaceous materials into valuable fuels and chemicals using renewable energy such as solar energy, electric energy, etc. [1–3]. The electroreduction of carbon dioxide is the most attractive way to convert CO2 to C1 products (CO, HCOOH, CH4) and C2 products (ethylene, ethanol, etc.) [4,5], because the reaction can be realized under mild conditions. At present, the research of electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide focuses on increasing energy efficiency (Faradaic efficiency and current efficiency), effectively reducing overpotential and achieving high current density [2,6]. Developing new efficient catalysts has always been considered as an effective way to solve the abovementioned problems.
Recently, many metal electrocatalysts, such as Ag [7,8], Au [9–11], Zn [12–14], Pd [6] have been identified to convert CO2 to CO. Metal nitrogen carbon catalyst (M=Ni [15,16],Fe [17]) and single-atom catalysts [18,19] are also research hotspots. In particularly, copper
electrode is a distinctive catalyst to catalyze CO2 to hydrocarbon because of its proper binding energy of *CO [20,21]. However, the poor selectivity of copper hinders further application of copper electrode. Therefore, many strategies have been developed to improve electrocatalysts, including defect engineering [22,23], changing geometric and electronic structures [24], doping engineering [5], morphology [25–27], size [28], vacancy [29], oxide-derived [30] etc.
Oxides or oxide-derived Cu catalysts is well structured to boost selectivity during electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction (ECR). Because Cu2O favors the formation of C2 products by promoting CeC coupling reaction [31], many works have been carried out on Cu2Obased catalysts. For example, synergistic effect between Cu(I) and Cu(0) in Cu@Cu2O improve the selectivity toward C2 products with FE of about 50% [32], and plasma-oxidized catalysts producing Cu+ enhance ethylene selectivity (60%) [33]. However, Cu2O layers formed at 500 °C exhibit a large surface roughness to produce CO and HCOOH [34]. Hence, the properties of Cu-based oxide layer greatly affect the catalytic selectivity.
In addition, introducing a second metallic element is considered as a more powerful approach to promote catalytic performance by changing intrinsic properties of pristine materials [35,36]. Elemental doping has

been proved to improve the selectivity and activity by designing charge redistribution [20], band structure [37], stabilizing valence state [5,38] and elevating d-band center [6,39] of the active sites. Therefore, Curich bimetallic catalysts have been used to enhance activity and selectivity of CO2 reduction. For example, Han’s group reported a Bdoped oxide-derived-Cu catalyst to improve the selectivity of C2H4 with FE of 48.2% [5]. Besides, the incorporation of Pd into Cu lattice upshifted the d-band center, increasing the binding energy of CO* protonation step for promoting the conversion of CO2 into CO [6]. Compared with pure copper catalysts, element doping inhibits some undesirable properties and exhibits others properties that favor specific pathways [40]. Many elements, such as Au [41,42], Ag [2], Pd [6,25], Sn [43,44], In [45], have been introduced into Cu to boost the conversion of CO2 to CO. Among these elements, In is a desirable one due to synergistic effect between Cu and In, which can enhance adsorption of *COOH and inhibit adsorption of *H [46,47]. Larrazábal et al. found that the presence of In(OH)3 layer in heterogeneous catalyst promotes the selectivity of CO. Since the catalytic reaction only occur on the surface, the surface composition design is particularly important [48]. Züttel et al. prepared Cu/In interface by annealing Cu(OH)2 nanowire wetted with indium salt solution, and the catalyst revealed 93% FE toward to CO with stability of 60 h [47]. However, the optimal current density of this catalyst is only 2.5mA cm−2 at −0.7 V vs RHE. And Cu/ In catalysts most have low current density [46,48,49]. Therefore, it is highly desired to develop a strategy for Cu/In catalysts to promote CO production with competitive current density. In this work, we developed a dendritic core-shell In-doped Cu@Cu2O catalyst by simple coelectrodeposition method on carbon fiber paper for high-efficiency selective electroreduction CO2 to CO. Because Indium is much less conductive than copper, only small amount of In element was doped to conductive Cu parent to enhance selectivity at high current density. The amount of doped In in catalysts was adjusted by tailoring indium ion concentration in electrodeposition solution. Superior electrocatalytic property was inclined to that indium doping caused increased intrinsic activity, which made catalysts be superior to CO reaction path.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: The carbon fiber paper (TGP-H-60, 0.19 nm thickness) was purchased from Toray. Anhydrous indium sulfate (In2(SO4)3, 99.99%, Aladdin), citric acid (C6H7O8, ≥ 99.5%, Aladdin), Copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O, ≥ 99%, Fengchuan chemical reagent technology co. LTD), Sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 96% ∼ 98%, Damao chemical reagent), Potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO3, 99.7–100.5% (dried basis), Alfa Aesar) were used. High-purity nitrogen-carbon dioxide mixed gas (99.999%) and Argon gas (99.9993%), high purity helium (99.9993%) were used as the feedstock and carrier gas. All reagents were used as received.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation of catalysts
sections.text:
The carbon fiber paper (CFP) was cut into small pieces (3 cm×1 cm) and washed with ethanol and ultra-pure water (18.2 MΩ) successively. The ultrasonically cleaned in 0.5M H2SO4 for 40min. And then CFP was impregnated in 0.5 M H2SO4 and heated at 60 ℃ for 1 h for hydrophilic and activation treatment. Before electrodeposition, the CFP was activated by cyclic voltammetry in 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature. The electrodeposited dendritic copper was prepared on CFP in a solution containing 0.01M CuSO4, 0.05M C6H7O8 and 1M H2SO4. The electrodeposition was performed at constant potential (−1.2 V vs SCE) for 500 s in a three-electrodes glass cell. The dendritic In-doped Cu@Cu2O electrode was prepared in an electrolyte mixing with 0.01M CuSO4, 0.05M C6H7O8 and 1M H2SO4 and x M In2(SO4)3 (Where x was set as 0.001, 0.003, 0.005). The time and
potential of deposition process were the same as the procedure of the Cu electrode. The electrodeposited indium electrode was performed at constant potential (-1.5 V vs SCE) for 500 s in a solution containing 0.005M In2(SO4)3, 0.05M C6H7O8 and 1M H2SO4. All electrodeposition experiments were carried out in a three-electrode glass cell with saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as reference electrode and Pt mesh as counter electrode at a water bath of 30 ℃.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterizations
sections.text: The In/Cu atomic ratio of In-doped Cu@Cu2O catalysts were measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, VISTA-MPX). The morphology of a series of catalysts was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, S-4800), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, jem-2100f) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM). X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern was collected on D/ MAX-2500 equipped with a Cu Kα X-ray source (λ = 0.1541 nm) at 40 kV and 40mA. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was determined by ESCALAB 250Xi using Al Kα X-ray source (hv = 1486.6 eV) and binding energy can be calibrated with C 1s spectra (binding energy = 284.8 eV).

sections.heading: 2.4. Electroreduction of CO2
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide was performed in a gas-tight glass H-Cell which had two compartments segregated by proton exchange membrane (Nafion 117, Dupont). The Ag/AgCl electrode was used as reference electrode, and platinum foil (1.5 cm×1.5 cm×0.1 cm) was applied as counter electrode. The catalyst on Carbon fiber paper was used as a working electrode. An aqueous solution containing 0.1M KHCO3 was used as the electrolyte. In the cathodic compartment, mass transfer was enhanced by mechanical agitation with a rotation rate of about 500 rpm. All experiments were carried out on the AutoLab (Model PGSTAT302 N) to control and collect electrochemical data. Before reduction, the gas mixture of 5% N2 and 95% CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte for 50min at 50ml min−1 to fully saturate the solution and remove air in system. During the electroreduction process, the gas flow rate was 40ml min−1, controlled by mass flow meter. Nitrogen was as the internal standard gas.
During electrolysis reaction, the gas products, carried by carbon dioxide, were analyzed by on-line gas chromatography (GC, GC-2010) equipped with barrier discharge ionization detector (BID) using high purity helium as carrier gas. After electrolysis, high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of liquid products.
The Faradaic efficiency (FE) for all products over In-doped Cu@Cu2O fluctuated around 100%. Bubbles sticking to the electrode surface was considered as a factor according to the literature [15]. The pressure of sample loops also had small uncertainties, leading to quantitative unsureness [50]. Therefore, we normalize Faradaic efficiency of In-doped Cu@Cu2O to show relative selectivity more clearly.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electrochemical characterizations
sections.text:
All the Electrochemical characterization were conducted in H-Cell with three-electrodes system. The electrolyte and electrodes were the same as that of the electrolysis process. Double layer capacitance of catalysts was determined by cyclic voltammetry scans in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 without stirring, and scanning potential range was between −0.22 ∼ −0.12 V vs RHE at the different sweep rates of 50, 100, 160, 220, 280mV s−1. The linearity is plotted about different current density versus scan rates at -0.27 V vs RHE, and the slope indicates the capacitance of the double layer. Double layer capacitance of pure-Cu and pure-In were measured similarly. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was carried out in Ar or CO2 saturated electrolyte, and
potential swept from 0.4 ∼ −0.8 V vs RHE at scan rate of 20mV s−1. At the optimal voltage of −0.8 V vs RHE, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurement was conducted in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 with an amplitude of 10mV from 0.1 to 105 Hz. The iR correction was applied for the LSV data.

sections.heading: 3.1. Effect of In doping on structure and morphology
sections.text:
Dendritic core-shell indium-doped Cu@Cu2O electrodes were synthesized by a co-electrodeposited method applied at a relatively high potential (−1.2 V vs SCE) on carbon fiber paper in acidic solution in Fig. 1. The structure of the resulting electrode was characterized by Xray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Fig. 2a, the diffraction characteristic peaks of the sample at 2θ=43°, 50°, 74° and 90° are attributed to (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of metal copper (JCPDS 01–1241), respectively. It can be observed that In incorporation doesn’t change the crystal phase of the original copper catalyst. However, the characteristic peak of (111) plane in 3.7% In-Cu sample shifts to the lower by 0.12° compared with pure-Cu. The lattice constant of (111) crystal facet for 3.7% In-Cu (3.632 Å) is larger than that of pure-Cu (Figure S3). This
indicates that In is successfully doped into the lattice of Cu [6,20,51] and In-Cu alloy is formed. Because the size of indium atom is bigger than that of copper atom, if In atom is doped into Cu lattice, the characteristic peak of Cu would shift negatively leading to larger lattice constant than that of pure-Cu.
To further analyze the chemical valence state, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were carried out. The XPS spectra of In 3d proves the existence of In (Fig. 2d). In Fig. 2b, the characteristic Cu 2p3/2 peak at 932.47 eV and 934.17 eV are attributed to Cu0,1+ and Cu2+, respectively [38]. The other two smaller peaks at 944 eV and 963 eV are satellite peaks of Cu2+. The main valence state of catalyst surface is Cu0, 1+, rather than Cu2+ resulted from the oxidation of surface exposed to air. Cu0 and Cu+ can’t be distinguish due to their very similar binding energy values. Hence, Cu L3M45M45 Auger spectra was done and shown in Fig. 2c. The peaks at ca. 916.3 eV and 918.4 eV are attributed to Cu+ and Cu0, respectively [44]. In Fig. S4b, the O 1s spectra peak at 530.5 eV is attributed Cu2O, which also shows the presence of Cu+ [30,52]. Interestingly, as observed in the Auger spectrum, Cu+ is predominant species rather than Cu0. However, the XRD pattern don’t reflect distinctive Cu2O characteristic peak. This indicates that the surface Cu2O is amorphous.
The morphology of the as-prepared catalysts was determined using
a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As shown in Fig. 3a and b, pure-Cu has a dendritic structure, while pure-In has an irregular block structure. As a result, dendritic pure-Cu catalyst has a larger surface area compared with block pure-In material. In-doped Cu@Cu2O materials inherit the dendritic structure of the pure-Cu catalyst, fortunately emerging completely different structure from pure-In (Fig. 3c). Compared with pureCu sample with above 200 nm tips, In incorporation obviously shrinks the size (Figs. 3d and S2). The 3.7% In-Cu sample forms a fully developed dendritic structure with tips that are approximately in range of 20∼50 nm in diameter. From Fig. 3e, it could be observed that the tip is wrapped in a 6 nm thick amorphous shell. The inner core is classified as copper phase with the typical lattice fringe of 0.209 nm assigned to Cu (111). Combining XRD and XPS, it can be deduced that core-shell structure was synthesized with external amorphous In-doped Cu2O layer and the internal In-doped Cu0 crystal phase. The EDS elemental mappings (Fig. 3g–j) clearly show a uniform distribution of In and O elements.
The catalytic performances of pure-Cu, In-doped Cu@Cu2O, pure-In catalysts were performed in H-Cell in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 to understand the effect of indium doping on enhancing CO selectivity and inhibiting hydrogen evolution. As shown in Fig. 4a, the FE towards CO is sharply promoted due to In doping in the range of -0.6 V to -0.9 V vs RHE. The FECO of 87.6 ± 2.2% are achieved over the 3.7% In-Cu electrocatalysts at -0.8 V vs RHE, which are 7 times and 3 times higher than that of pure-Cu (11.1%) and pure-In (20.9%), respectively. Within the range of potentials being studied, the FEs of pure-Cu and pure-In samples are below 14% and 24% toward CO, respectively. As shown in Figure S6a, hydrogen evolution is the main reaction for pure-Cu catalyst and FE exceeds 90%, which mean that pure-Cu has a strong hydrogen evolution nature. Similarly, HER is also preferred for pure-In electrode (Figure S6b). Besides, the current density is also one of the main parameters to evaluate the catalytic performance. As shown in Fig. 3b, the partial current density of CO over 3.7% In-Cu
(9.7 ± 1.04mA cm−2) is larger than that over pure-Cu (1.13mA cm−2) and pure-In (0.41mA cm−2) catalysts during ECR. Both total and partial current density of pure-In sample are very weak among all the samples (Figure S5a and b), which illustrates that neither hydrogen nor carbon dioxide reduction has fast reaction rate. The boost of catalytic performance of In-doped Cu@Cu2O, confirms that the combination of Cu and In enhances CO selectivity by inhibiting hydrogen evolution [46].
Fig. 4d shows the LSV curves performed in CO2 or Ar-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3. The current density of pure-Cu in Ar-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 is higher than that of 3.7% In-Cu indicating the inhibition of hydrogen evolution by In doping. The current density of pure-Cu in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 is lower than that in Ar-saturated one due to the adsorption of intermediates on electrode surface during ECR [47]. In CO2-saturated electrolyte, In doping electrode can significantly increase the current density, indicating the distinct boost of ECR by In doping.
In order to study the stability of 3.7% In-Cu catalyst, long-term electrolysis was evaluated at −0.8 V vs RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 (Fig. 4d). After 4 h, the total current density only has a slight increase and maintain high Faradaic efficiency, which could be attributed to the dendritic core-shell In-doped Cu@Cu2O structure. Then, XPS characterization was carried out to investigate the surface valence states of Cu after the reduction process. In Fig. 4d, the characteristic Cu 2p3/2 peak at 933.9 eV is attributed to Cu2+. The Cu L3M45M45 Auger spectra confirms the presence of Cu0 (918.4 eV) on the catalyst surface (Fig. 4f). As shown in Figure S11, the oxidation/reduction potentials of Cu in pure-Cu and 3.7% In-Cu samples are larger than -0.6 V vs RHE. During the reduction process at -0.8 V vs RHE, Cu+ species will be reduced to Cu0. This also indicates that Cu2+ species in the used samples are ascribed to the air oxidation due to the exposure in air after test. Additionally, the dendritic morphology of 3.7% In-Cu after longterm stability test isn’t destroyed (Figure S10a).

sections.heading: 3.2. The role of In content on ECR performance
sections.text:
To further study the role of indium content on ECR performance, Indoped Cu@Cu2O samples varied with composition were produced by adjusting the concentration of In2(SO4)3 in solution under the same content of copper ion (0.01M). The actual composition of as-prepared catalysts was measured by using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP - OES). As shown in Table S1, the Cu/In ratios decrease with the increased indium content in solution, thus, a series of catalysts can be recorded as pure-Cu, 1.6% In-Cu, 3.7% In-Cu, 7.1% In-Cu, pure-In, respectively.
Firstly, the dendritic morphology is also different to some extent with increased In content, and morphological evolution is recorded in Fig. 5. When the In content is as low as 1.6%, the branches are not fully developed with many irregular edges and corners (Fig. 5a). SEM image in Fig. 5b manifests that the 3.7% In-Cu likes a stem covered with pointed “leaves”. With further increase in indium content, the structure resembles the stacked configuration of irregular nanoparticles with uneven surfaces. Secondly, as shown in Fig. 5d, In incorporation does not change the crystal phase. From the enlarged diffraction pattern in Fig. 5e, it could be observed that the main characteristic peak significantly shifts to the left in different degrees as the In content
increases. Compared with pure-Cu sample, it can observed that phase deviation increased first and then decreased, probably due to aggregation with further increase in indium content hindering Indium to be doped into Cu lattice [53]. The 3.7% In-Cu has maximum phase deviation because the lattice constant of 3.7% In-Cu is largest (Figure S3). Therefore, the appropriate indium content of the feed solution is expected to increase the indium doping levels for enhancing the selectivity of CO. Then, different from pure-Cu, In-doped Cu2O layer is formed after oxyphilic In doping. As shown in Fig. 5f, the ratio of surface Cu+/Cu0 varies significantly as the increase of In content. 3.7% In-Cu shows the highest ratio of Cu+/Cu0. On the contrary, the ratio of Cu+/Cu0 of pure-Cu is smallest. This indicates that In doping can well regulate the surface composition distribution of Cu+/Cu0. At low doping level, the reduction of cuprous oxides is gradually inhibited by In doping probably due to the formation of Cu-In oxides alloy. But at high doping level, the alloying of Cu-In species is restrained leading to the decrease of surface Cu+/Cu0 ratio.
Finally, the peaks in In 3d spectra of In-doped Cu@Cu2O samples shifts to lower binding energy resulting in charge redistribution and strong electronic interaction between Cu and In. The binding energy of In 3d5/2 electrons is recorded at 446.12 eV and 444.1 eV attributed to In3+ and In0, respectively [54]. And In2O3 is the main species on pureIn surface. XRD curve doesn’t reflect distinctive In2O3 characteristic peaks, indicating its amorphous structure. Compared with pure-In sample, the binging energy of In3+ state of In-doped Cu@Cu2O samples shift negatively by 0.66 ∼ 1.37 eV because the electronegative of Indium is slightly higher than that of copper, resulting in charge redistribution [20]. Among all In-doped Cu@Cu2O samples, the 3.7% In-Cu has the maximum charge redistribution compared with other samples. According to the above analysis, we can deduce that the overall electronic structure of In-doped Cu@Cu2O active sites is modified due to the charge redistribution, which boosts the electrocatalytic performance.
To further study the relationship between indium content and catalytic performance, FE and current density toward CO against In
content at the dominant potential (-0.8 V vs RHE) was plotted as volcano curves in Fig. 6a and 6b. 3.7% In-Cu sample shows the highest FECO of 87.6± 2.2 % and partial current density of 9.7 ± 1.04 mA cm−2 with a total current density of 11.1 ± 0.85mA cm-2, which is competitive with previously reported copper indium electrode materials (Table S2). While the FE over 7.1% In-Cu sample reduces to 74.9 ± 4.6% at -0.8 V vs RHE, which reveal that more In content leads to less improvement of selectivity. Both total current density and CO partial current density of 3.7% In-Cu sample are larger than that of other samples (Fig. 6b). For pure-Cu, the current density is mainly contributed by HER. The core-shell In-doped Cu@Cu2O inherits the high current density partially due to the metallic Cu core. Compared with pure-Cu and pure-In samples, the by-products (HCOOH and H2) over In-doped Cu@Cu2O are greatly suppressed (Fig. 6a). During electrolysis Cu2O can be reduced to metallic Cu whose surfaces have active sites for ECR, but the original oxide layer also contributes to the transient changes in the CO2 product distribution [34]. In addition, in ECR reaction only surface atoms can be utilized [26]. Therefore, the surface structure of catalyst plays a vital role on catalytic performance. As shown in Fig. 6c, the selectivity and partial current density significantly depend on the ratio of Cu+/Cu0 of Cu-base catalysts. As the Cu+/Cu0 ratio increases from 1 (pure-Cu sample) to 2.2 (1.6%In-Cu sample), the FECO value dramatically increases from 11% up to 83.2 ± 3.3%. Further increasing the Cu+/Cu0 ratio to 2.6 (3.7%In-Cu sample), the FECO value further increases about 4.4%. This suggests that the Cu+/Cu0 ratio derived from In doping significantly affect the intrinsic activity of the active sites and dominate the catalytic performance, which is consistent with the ref [30]. The near linear relationship between partial current density and Cu+/Cu0 ratio at low In doping (≤3.7% with Cu+/Cu0 ratio of 2.6) further confirms that the active sites depend on the initial Cu+/Cu0 mixed state of as-deposited catalysts derived from In doping. But when the Cu+/Cu0 ratio decrease back to 2.2 (7.1% In-Cu sample), the FE value and partial current density significantly decrease, lower than that for 1.6%In-Cu sample. This is probably that at high In doping level, part of low active In
couldn’t dope into the Cu lattice to form the active Cu-In alloy species from the XPS and XRD results, which decrease the electrochemically active surface area (active sites) of the catalyst. Therefore, the FE and jCO of 7.1% In-Cu sample are significantly lower than that of 1.6%In-Cu samples although they have the similar Cu+/Cu0 ratio. 3.7% In-Cu sample with the highest ratio of Cu+/Cu0 shows the highest FECO and partial current density. The excellent catalytic performance may be attributed to the difference of intrinsic activity of Cu0 from copper oxides reduction in different initial oxides layer [34]. Cu produced by electroreduction Cu2O layer can enhance the conversion of CO2 to CO at low potential and the Cu2O incorporated into the p-block elements (such as Sn, In) can promote the conversion of CO2 to CO [34,55]. Previous study has shown that, during reduction process of Cu2O to Cu, the generation of lattice fragmentation [31,56], defect sites [57], morphology reconstruction [58] surface reconstruction [59] is critical for improving catalyst performance. The intrinsic activity of Cu0 produced from Cu2O is different from that of the original copper. Therefore, the presence of In-doped Cu2O layer plays an important role on enhancing the reactivity for CO2 to CO due to the altered surface structures after its electrochemical reduction.
In-doped Cu@Cu2O materials inherit the dendritic structure of the pure-Cu catalyst. With the increase of In content, the catalysts showed the similar crystal size with slightly evolved shape. But the crystalline structure of these catalysts did not change according to the XRD results in Fig. 5. Therefore, the change of size and shape mainly induced an evolution in the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA), i.e. the number of active sites. In order to obtain the ECSA, the cyclic voltammetry for these electrodes was firstly carried out to get double-layer capacitance. The double-layer capacitance is summarized in Fig. 6d. The double-layer capacitance of 3.7% In-Cu sample is 1.63, 1.08, 1.45 and 24.14 times higher than that of pure-Cu, 1.6% In-Cu, 7.1% In-Cu and pure-In samples, respectively. The roughness factor (Rf) is obtained by normalizing the capacitance values by that of smooth flat metal such as metallic copper (CS= 29 μF cm−2 [60]). The ECSA can be calculated by multiplying the roughness factor by the geometric area (ECSA=Ageom ·Rf). For all catalysts, the geometric areas are equal. As shown in Table S3, large roughness factor (Rf) corresponds to large ECSA. In order to further compare intrinsic activity, the partial current density is normalized to the ECSA. As shown in Fig. 6b, pure-Cu sample has a low intrinsic activity for producing CO. The normalized current density substantially increases with indium content, and then the increase of normalized current density gradually slows down and finally becomes stable. These means that the intrinsic activity is improved by a small amount (≤1.6%) of indium doping. While further increase of indium content (1.6% ∼ 3.7%), the growth trend of intrinsic activity slows down. And intrinsic activity could not further improve when the amount of doped indium is greater than 3.7%.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed to measure charge transfer resistance. As shown in Figure S8, charge transfer resistances of In-doped Cu@Cu2O catalysts are lower than that of pure-Cu and pure In samples. The 3.7% In-Cu has the minimum charge transfer resistance of 6.6 Ω, indicating the accelerated chargetransfer process during ECR. And the pure-In shows the maximum charge transfer resistance of 160 Ω, resulting in the small current density.
To better understand the effect on reaction kinetics by indium doping, Tafel plots are analyzed and summarized in Figure S9f. The Tafel slope of all samples is greater than 118 mv dec−1 [60], and 3.7% In-Cu has a smaller Tafel slope (130.2 mv dec−1) than that of other Cubase samples. This illuminates that the rate determining step is the single electron transfer process (CO2 + e→ CO2−) [3,60]. According to literature, In sites can block the adsorption of *H to inhibit hydrogen evolution [45]. And DFT manifests that Cu and In synergy may decrease energy barrier of key intermediate *COOH, which helps produce CO [47]. Moreover, the oxyphilic metals In incorporated into the copper lattice can better stabilize the intermediate *COOH through enhancing
interaction with O-ends of *COOH [20,61].Therefore, when In atom is doped into Cu lattice, the properties of Cu-based materials are modified. Subsequently, adsorption energy of *H and *COOH over the Indoped Cu electrocatalysts might be changed to enhance the conversion of CO2 to CO and suppress H2 evolution.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, dendritic In-doped Cu@Cu2O electrode of various compositions is synthetized by a maneuverable co-electrodeposition method on low-cost carbon paper. The catalytic performance of ECR is tailored by controlling the In-doped content. In doping can increase Faradaic efficiency of CO significantly and achieve high current density. The enhanced catalytic activity may be mainly attributed to the charge re-distribution and the formation of In-doped Cu2O layer due to In doping, which lead to the increase of intrinsic activity. The ratio of Cu+/Cu0, charge distribution, morphology and electrochemical active area (ECSA) can be adjusted by doped indium content. The Cu+/Cu0
ratio play a vital role on enhancing Faradaic efficiency and partial current density of CO. Consequently, a small amount of indium incorporation can suppress hydrogen evolution and greatly improves selectivity of CO. Copper modified by indium doping strengthens the adsorption of *COOH via enhancing interaction with O-ends of *COOH and hinders the adsorption of *H, leading to high selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO.
